processing: An oven-dried green tea (hongqing) made in four steps: withering spread, fixing, rolling and baking dry.
harvest_season: Generally spring tea only, with picking from early March to a standard of one bud and two leaves.
appearance_dry: Tight, sturdy, even strands with sharp tips, thickly covered in white down.
appearance_wet: Tender, even leaves that open into whole bud-and-leaf sets.
taste_profile: Rich, thick and clean with a strong fresh aroma, then a mouth-watering returning sweetness; more weight than most Chinese greens.

brewing.notes: Ordinary starting points for a downy large-leaf green. It is known for standing up to several steeps; the down can cloud the first one slightly, which is normal.

vintage_note: Sold as a spring tea, picked from March, and best drunk within the year like other Chinese greens. Ask for the current year's picking; the name has been in use since the 1980s, and little is documented about grading on today's market.
description:
Nannuo Baihao takes its name from Nannuo Mountain in Menghai, better known to most tea drinkers for pu-erh and old trees. This is the mountain's other face: a modern downy green tea, oven-dried rather than sun-dried.

That single difference matters. Pu-erh raw material is sun-dried, while this tea is baked dry after fixing and rolling, which gives a cleaner, more fragrant green and little reason to age it. Large-leaf buds are hairy by nature, which is where the baihao, or white down, comes from.

The cup is bright yellow-green with a generous aroma and a thicker, stronger taste than an eastern green. It leaves a lingering sweetness and lasts several steeps. Do not treat it like pu-erh: boiling water flattens it.

It belongs to the wider family of Yunnan oven-dried greens, Dianlv, where it counts among the better-known named products. Look for plentiful down and whole, even strands.

If you like the idea, try it beside a young sheng from the same mountain, which shows what drying and intent do to similar leaf.
history:
Unlike many famous names, this one is recent and dated: Nannuo Baihao was created in 1981. In June 1982 it was among the thirty national famous teas chosen at a selection held by the Ministry of Commerce, and accounts say it was named two years running.

The mountain's own fame helped, since Nannuo is promoted as home of a celebrated old tea tree. Who actually developed the tea is not well documented.
